Reading pension statistics: count the plans, count the members and check the dates

Explore four charts from an official Canadian pension-table snapshot, with a reference-year selector, separate count scales and a reconciled funding-instrument breakdown.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

Plan counts and active-member counts describe different quantities. Their dates, units and classifications must be clear before the numbers can inform a planning question.

01

Start with the two things being counted

Statistics Canada’s Table 11-10-0099-01 reports registered pension plans, active members and asset measures across several dimensions. This article selects Canada, total registered pension plans and the count statistics for plans and active members, both sexes. It does not select the table’s percentage or asset-value measures.

For the 2025 table reference, the selected plan count is 15,762 and the reported active-member count is 7,352,686. Those figures have different units. They cannot be added to form a meaningful total, and one should not be labelled as the other.

A reported member count also is not a dollar amount or an annual pension quote. It cannot show how much a particular household will receive in retirement. The charts provide context for understanding the pension system, while an individual plan statement supplies a different kind of evidence.

02

The January reference date does not put every measure on the same day

The source metadata distinguishes its reporting clocks. The number of plans and their terms refer to 1 January. Membership relates to the plan’s year-end in the preceding calendar year, normally 31 December. A column headed 2025 therefore does not make every membership observation a live count on 1 January 2025.

The charts retain the publisher’s table reference years from 2021 through 2025. Their titles and notes identify the membership timing, rather than silently relabelling it as a current 2026 observation. The snapshot was released on 28 July 2026 and checked on 25 October 2026.

The reference-year control changes which columns of that fixed snapshot are displayed. It does not request fresh observations or extend the data into later years. Starting the control at 2022 retains at least two reference points for the comparisons, while every index continues to use the same 2021 baseline.

03

Compare changes on an index, then return to the absolute counts

The 2021 reference contains 16,359 plans and 6,593,256 reported active members. By the 2025 reference, the plan count is lower by 597 while the reported membership is higher by 759,430. The direction of one quantity does not determine the direction of the other.

The first chart divides each series by its own 2021 value and multiplies by 100. Both begin at 100, allowing their proportional changes to be read on one index scale. An index of 110 means that a series is 10% above its own starting value. It does not mean 110% of employees are covered.

The index chart uses a declared 95–115 vertical range to make the proportional movements visible. The second and third charts keep the original counts on separate scales. This avoids plotting roughly sixteen thousand plans and several million members on the same absolute axis, which would make one series visually disappear. The zero-based plan bars also keep modest differences in plan counts in proportion.

The pattern alone does not establish why counts changed. A change in the organisation or composition of plans could matter, but attributing the observed difference to a specific cause would require further evidence. These figures do not follow one worker through a career.

04

Read a funding category as a classification, not a benefit promise

The final chart groups reported members by funding instrument for the selected reference year. The metadata describes the funding instrument through the legal or contractual arrangement used to hold and invest contributions.

There are six direct categories below the total in the selected hierarchy. The insurance-company-contract total has more detailed subcategories of its own. Adding those children again alongside their parent would count the same category membership twice, so the graphic uses only the six direct categories.

The curated extract checks that those six values sum to the published active-member total for every displayed reference year. For the 2025 reference, the trust-agreement category reports 4,276,098 active members; that is a category count, not a personal account balance.

This classification answers a different question from defined-benefit versus defined-contribution design. It also does not describe an equity/bond allocation or the quality of a provider. A funding label cannot replace the actual plan terms when you need to understand investment responsibility, benefit calculation or access to money.

05

Translate the statistical question into the personal records you need

Before using a national figure in a personal plan, identify the missing information. To measure a share of employed people, you would need a suitable employment denominator and matching definitions and periods. Dividing these counts by an unrelated population figure would not establish that coverage rate.

To estimate retirement cash, obtain the administrator’s actual benefit statement or account information, expected payment dates, applicable options and a separate tax assessment. Keep a capital balance distinct from an annual pension payment. No national member count supplies those details.

  1. Write down the measure, unit, reference date and population.
  2. Use the original count scale for magnitudes and a declared baseline for proportional changes.
  3. Check whether category totals and subcategories overlap.
  4. Identify what additional evidence is needed for the household decision.
  5. Recheck the public table for revisions before treating a snapshot as current.

The four graphics support this reading process. They do not estimate a personal entitlement, forecast future membership, calculate a worker-coverage probability or recommend a pension option.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four graphics use a curated public Statistics Canada snapshot from Table 11-10-0099-01, released 28 July 2026. The first graphic rebases each reported series to its own 2021 reference value; the other graphics show reported counts. The year control filters that snapshot, with no forecast or personal pension calculation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 11-10-0099-01 ↗

    Released 28 July 2026; official full-table CSV and metadata downloaded and checked 25 October 2026. Forty selected count observations cover references 2021–2025: five plan totals, five member totals and thirty top-level funding-category member counts. The source metadata distinguishes January plan dates from preceding-plan-year membership. Percentage and asset-value rows are excluded.

  2. Statistics Canada · Full-table CSV and metadata ↗

    The reproducible extraction checks dimensions, number/units scaling, missingness, status flags, duplicates, the category hierarchy and reconciliation for every reference year. The first chart’s index values are independent calculations from the published counts. Raw source files remain outside the deployed website.
